title: 10 Accidental Inventions: By the Numbers
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant count down a top-ten list of accidental inventions: LSD (Albert Hofmann's accidental dose and 'bicycle day'), corn flakes (John Harvey and Will Keith Kellogg at the Battle Creek sanitarium), dynamite (Alfred Nobel, nitroglycerin, kieselguhr), saccharin (Constantine Fahlberg and Ira Remsen at Johns Hopkins), Viagra (sildenafil trial side effect), Velcro (George de Mestral), penicillin (Alexander Fleming), and anesthesia (ether and nitrous oxide, laughing gas parties). The episode also includes a plug segment for a horror fiction contest and a listener mail story about medical marijuana in a family history.

segments.title: Opening banter and LSD
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about top-ten lists, then discuss the accidental discovery of LSD by Albert Hofmann, including his bicycle ride home and his later views on the drug.

segments.title: Corn flakes
segments.summary: Discussion of how Will Keith Kellogg, working with his brother John Harvey Kellogg at the Battle Creek Sanitarium, accidentally made corn flakes from a boiled wheat dough left out too long, later switching to corn.

segments.title: Dynamite
segments.summary: Alfred Nobel's work with nitroglycerin, the accident that led him to mix it with kieselguhr, the stabilized explosive he made, and the Nobel Peace Prize legacy. Hosts also distinguish dynamite from TNT.

segments.title: Saccharin
segments.summary: Constantine Fahlberg, working in Ira Remsen's lab at Johns Hopkins, tasted sweetness on bread after not washing his hands, leading to the discovery and patent of saccharin; discussion of its zero food energy and changing health approval.

segments.title: Viagra
segments.summary: Development of Viagra from a heart and angina drug trial in which participants reported erections as a side effect; hosts mention sales figures and competitors.

segments.title: Velcro
segments.summary: George de Mestral noticed burrs sticking to his dog after an Alps hike, recreated the hook-and-loop system with nylon, and spent about ten years before manufacturing it successfully. Hosts discuss the name's French origins and cheap imitations.

segments.title: Penicillin
segments.summary: Alexander Fleming noticed a mold killing bacteria in a petri dish after vacation; the strain could not be mass produced until Florey, Heatley and Mowyer found one that grew well. Hosts discuss finishing antibiotic courses.

segments.title: Anesthesia and laughing gas parties
segments.summary: Nineteenth-century laughing gas and ether parties led to the accidental discovery of anesthesia by Crawford Long, William Morton, Charles Jackson and Horace Wells. Hosts describe early surgery without anesthesia and mention a flesh-eating bacteria news story.

segments.title: Plug: horror fiction contest and Comic-Con
segments.summary: Hosts promote the horror fiction contest (submissions June 18 to July 20, 3,000 to 4,000 words, U.S. residents only) and a planned Comic-Con panel.

segments.title: Listener mail: medical marijuana family story
segments.summary: A listener shares how her father's doctor suggested marijuana during chemotherapy in the early eighties, and how relatives smuggled it, and the hosts respond.
